A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the EET current of anode-respirating G. sulfurreductens cells is controlled by the electron-transfer rate between the outer membrane cytochromes and the electrode surface, and that the electron-transfer rate is limited in the potential region positive to E(m) of a redox peak.
EET of an anode-respiring microbe can be controlled by the redox properties of the solid-state anode, as well as the redox properties and concentrations of soluble mediators.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the NFR characteristic of anode-respirers may be a general feature for EET to solid-state accepters, and the EET of anodic bacteria can be controlled by the redox potential of extracellular electron acceptors.
the E(m) value of a redox peak is not a reliable indicator of EET activity in electroactive bacteria.
